## Why This Is Asked
This tests practical, beginner-friendly ability to diagnose and mitigate I/O scheduling bottlenecks in a multi-tenant Linux environment using standard observability tools and per-tenant controls, with a safe rollback plan.

## Key Concepts
- I/O scheduling on NVMe devices (mq-deadline, kyber)
- cgroup v2 I/O controls (io.max, io.weight)
- Multi-queue block devices and NUMA awareness
- Observability: iostat, iotop, blktrace, fio
- Safe rollback and validation criteria

## Code Example
```bash
# switch scheduler
echo kyber > /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/scheduler
# verify
cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/scheduler
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you verify the per-tenant isolation remains intact under burst?
- What instrumentation would you add to prevent regressions in future bursts?

## Why This Is Asked
Multi-tenant logging can cause IO contention and latency spikes when many small writers share a single path. This question tests practical isolation, rotation, and QoS strategies without changing app code.

## Key Concepts
- Systemd sandboxing: PrivateTmp, PrivateDevices, ReadOnlyPaths
- Per-tenant log isolation and rotation using logrotate
- Disk I/O control: ionice and IO scheduling
- Quotas: per-tenant quotas on a dedicated log volume (e.g., project quotas on XFS)
- Test plan: simulate bursts and verify rollback safety

## Code Example
```ini
; /etc/systemd/system/ci-agent@.service
[Unit]
Description=CI Agent for tenant %i

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/ci-agent --tenant=%i
PrivateTmp=true
PrivateDevices=true
ReadOnlyPaths=/var/log/ci
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_SYSLOG
IOSchedulingClass=idle
IOSchedulingPriority=7
```

```bash
; /etc/logrotate.d/ci-agent-%i
/var/log/ci/tenant-*/agent.log {
  size 50M
  rotate 7
  copytruncate
  missingok
  notifempty
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you validate per-tenant isolation under peak bursts? 
- Which metrics would you monitor to detect drift or misconfigurations, and how would you roll back safely?

## Why This Question Is Asked

This question evaluates the ability to design production-grade controls for cross-tenant I/O contention in storage-bound workloads—a common challenge in shared infrastructure environments.

## Key Concepts

- cgroup v2 I/O quota control (io.max)
- Per-tenant block-device isolation
- NUMA-aware memory caching
- io_uring tuning for asynchronous I/O
- Observability with iostat, blktrace, bpftool/bpftrace
- Staged load testing with canaries and rollback

## Implementation Example

```bash
# Set per-tenant I/O throttle (500 MB/s limit)
echo "254:0 524288000" > /sys/fs/cgroup/<tenant-group>/io.max

# Verify the throttle is applied
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/<tenant-group>/io.max

# Monitor with iostat for latency distribution
iostat -x 1

# Trace block I/O with blktrace
blktrace -d /dev/nvme0n1 -o /tmp/blktrace

# Use bpftrace to observe I/O latency distribution
bpftrace -e 'kprobe:blk_mq_start_request { @start[ctx->regs->di] = nsecs; }
kprobe:blk_mq_complete_request { @latency = hist(nsecs - @start[ctx->regs->di]); }'
```
